title: Copper’s Grip On AI Scaling Is Starting To Slip
gist: Copper is losing its monopoly on AI scale-up interconnect: at 200-gig signaling copper tops out around 5-7 meters, so fiber is now entering scale-up domains that stretch beyond a single rack, while optical circuit switching — proven inside Google's Jupiter network at 40% less power and 30% less cost — is being evaluated by other operators for the upper tiers of leaf-and-spine fabrics. Nvidia's $2B stakes in Lumentum and Coherent and Lightmatter's NVLink entry signal the money is already repositioning toward photonics, though no one outside Google has deployed OCS.

insights.claim: The industry rule of thumb that scale-up means copper and scale-out means optical is dissolving, as rising data rates push copper into loss, reach, and power limits even inside a single rack.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Copper cable and connector suppliers face a structurally shrinking share of the fastest-growing part of the AI rack; optical component names capture the incremental socket.
insights.quote: The old rule that scale-up is copper and scale-out is optical is starting to blur
insights.locator: Data-center network fabrics are undergoing

insights.claim: Of scale-up's three historical defining traits — single rack, copper wiring, and memory semantics — only memory semantics survives, meaning a scale-up domain is now defined purely as one operating-system domain with a single memory address space regardless of physical media.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Reframe scale-up TAM around addressable memory domains rather than rack counts — the addressable interconnect market extends past the rack boundary.
insights.quote: Software guys define scale-up as one operating system domain where they have one memory
insights.locator: Scale-up as previously defined had three elements

insights.claim: A fourth scaling tier called 'scale-in' — bandwidth leaving the GPU that stays inside a single chassis — entered industry vocabulary only in the last three months, creating a new discrete layer of interconnect spend below the rack.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: A newly named layer usually precedes a newly named product category and standards body — watch for scale-in-specific IP and connector announcements.
insights.quote: This a new term that has only started in the last three months
insights.locator: Scaling evolves yet further

insights.claim: The AI data-center interconnect hierarchy now has four distinct tiers with distinct media: scale-in inside a server or board, scale-up within (and now beyond) a rack using memory semantics, scale-out between racks over Ethernet RDMA, and scale-across between campuses over fiber.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Use the four-tier map to attribute vendor revenue: each tier has different attach rates for copper, optics, switching silicon, and IP.
insights.locator: The definitions of these up until recently

insights.claim: Compute clusters are outgrowing the single rack and recruiting servers in adjacent racks, which lengthens interconnect runs and pulls fiber into scale-up domains that were previously all-copper.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Scale-up cabling becomes a mixed copper-plus-fiber bill of materials, raising optical attach per GPU beyond current scale-out-only models.
insights.quote: If it’s going to be within a rack, you’re probably going to use copper
insights.locator: Aside from the addition of scale-in

insights.claim: At a 200-gig signaling rate copper is viable only to roughly five meters, seven if pushed hard, and past ten meters optics is mandatory — a hard physical boundary that sets the crossover point for optical attach.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: This is the single most tradeable number in the article: any rack architecture requiring >10m accelerator-to-accelerator reach converts to optics by physics, not preference.
insights.quote: Certainly, once you hit 10 meters and beyond, it absolutely has to be optics.
insights.locator: In terms of how long a link requires optics

insights.claim: The UALink standard hard-codes single-switch-hop accelerator-to-accelerator connectivity even when a scale-up domain spans multiple racks, so cross-rack expansion does not require an extra switch-to-switch tier.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: UALink's topology guarantee removes a key architectural objection to multi-rack scale-up, accelerating the exact use case that requires optics.
insights.quote: UALink scale-up fabrics are designed to maintain single-switch-hop accelerator-to-accelerator connectivity
insights.locator: The one-hop expectation for scale-up

insights.claim: Inside a scale-up domain every GPU is one hop from every other GPU, versus roughly two hops for scale-out — the hop-count differential is what makes scale-up domains worth their cost premium.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Hop count is the proxy metric for latency-sensitive AI performance; architectures that add hops to gain reach trade away the scale-up value proposition.
insights.quote: Within the scale-up domain, every GPU is just one hop away from every other GPU
insights.locator: Typical implementations of scale-up and scale-out

insights.claim: Reports cite GPUs running at roughly 25% efficiency because they sit idle waiting for data, making interconnect latency — not FLOPS — the binding constraint on realized AI compute.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: If utilization is really ~25%, interconnect vendors are selling a 4x effective-compute multiplier — a far better ROI story than incremental silicon.
insights.quote: There have been a lot of reports on the efficiency of these GPUs that are maybe 25% efficient because they’re just sitting there waiting for data
insights.locator: Lower latency drives all of this

insights.claim: Google alone among major operators does not run a leaf-and-spine AI network, instead using a torus in which every TPU links to adjacent TPUs in three directions, giving the fabric a systolic character.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Google's fabric requires fundamentally different switching and optical components than the merchant leaf-and-spine market — its supply chain is not a read-through to Nvidia-based buildouts.
insights.quote: Google doesn’t have a leaf and spine network
insights.locator: Network architectures

insights.claim: Leaf-and-spine delivers a one-hop path between any two servers while a torus path can take four or more hops depending on node location, so torus fabrics pay a latency tax that only optical and circuit switching can offset.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Topology choice determines whether OCS is economically compelling — many-hop fabrics get the largest power savings from eliminating conversions.
insights.locator: A key difference between the two

insights.claim: Because optical technology cannot read packets, every hop in a packet-switched optical network forces an optical-to-electrical-to-optical conversion, and those repeated conversions are the dominant source of latency, energy, and cost in AI data-center fabrics.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: The O-E-O loop is the specific cost pool that OCS attacks; size the opportunity as transceiver count plus switch ASIC plus their cooling.
insights.quote: That optical-electrical-optical loop burns an enormous amount of power, adds latency, and drives up cost in data centers.
insights.locator: Packets to the rescue

insights.claim: Google is already migrating its AI network off the torus toward a dragonfly configuration, indicating even the most committed OCS operator considers current topology a moving target.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Topology churn at the largest custom-silicon operator means component demand mixes can shift abruptly between generations.
insights.quote: they’re moving from a torus network to yet another configuration called a dragonfly
insights.locator: Google’s OCS is a done deal

insights.claim: Optical circuit switching replaces packet routers with adjustable MEMS mirrors that reflect laser light from source fiber to destination fiber, eliminating optical-electrical conversions entirely along the reserved path.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: OCS displaces transceivers and switch ASICs with mirrors — a direct revenue substitution risk for merchant switch silicon vendors.
insights.quote: The company uses nothing but adjustable MEMS mirrors at each router.
insights.locator: Google’s implementation

insights.claim: Google began investigating the optical-electrical-optical power problem about 15 years ago and shipped a MEMS-based optical circuit switch about 10 years ago, giving it roughly a decade of deployed operational lead over the rest of the industry.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: A ten-year head start on a hardware-plus-control-plane system is a durable moat; competitors buying merchant OCS start far behind on operational software.
insights.quote: About 15 years ago, Google started looking at this, and about 10 years ago, made it happen with a MEMS [microelectromechanical systems]-based optical circuit switch.
insights.locator: Packets to the rescue

insights.claim: OCS power savings come from three stacked eliminations — roughly half the transceivers, the liquid cooling those transceivers required, and the switch's own ASIC and electronics — not from a single efficiency gain.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Each eliminated element is a supplier's revenue line; quantify OCS adoption risk against transceiver, cooling, and switch-silicon vendors simultaneously.
insights.quote: You’re eliminating half of the transceivers, eliminating the liquid cooling that’s required, and then the ASIC/electronics that are in the switch itself
insights.locator: The power savings reflect a number of changes

insights.claim: OCS is a workload-specific optimization that only pays off for long 'elephant flows' between a fixed source and destination, because setup and teardown overhead would dominate short bursty 'mice flows'.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: OCS demand tracks large-model training and inference traffic patterns, not general cloud traffic — it is a leveraged bet on frontier AI workloads specifically.
insights.quote: Optical circuit switching makes sense for ‘elephant flows,’ a term that I’ve been hearing others use
insights.locator: If this approach were taken for short

insights.claim: OCS requires a second, slower Ethernet-based control network to configure the mirrors before payload transmission, functionally reprising the telephone system's Signaling System 7 architecture inside the data center.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: The control plane is a low-cost commodity layer, so OCS does not carry a hidden second switching-capex burden that would kill its TCO case.
insights.quote: You have a lower-bandwidth Ethernet network to reconfigure the switches and the data route
insights.locator: A new Signaling System

insights.claim: The limiting factor on how quickly an OCS path can be reconfigured is transceiver lock time, not the reconfiguration of the switches themselves — pushing the technical bottleneck onto optical component vendors.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Faster-locking transceivers would widen the range of flows OCS can serve — a specific technical milestone to watch for expanding the addressable market.
insights.quote: It’s the transceiver lock that’s the bottleneck
insights.locator: It doesn’t take too long to reconfigure

insights.claim: The Ethernet control plane adds little capital cost because commodity low-bandwidth Ethernet switches serve only as a simple command center rather than carrying payload traffic.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Undermines the objection that running two networks doubles cost — supports the retrofit economics argument.
insights.quote: Ethernet switches are cheap. The Ethernet switch is just a simple low-bandwidth command center.
insights.locator: It may seem more complex to replace one network with two

themes.theme: Google's Jupiter as the proof point

insights.claim: Google's Jupiter network, after eight years of integrating OCS and wave division multiplexing with its SDN architecture, reported 10% lower flow completion, 30% higher throughput, 40% less power, 30% less cost, and 50x less downtime versus the best-known alternatives.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: These are the reference numbers every competing operator will underwrite an OCS business case against — a 40% network power reduction is material when power is the binding data-center constraint.
insights.quote: Jupiter does all this while reducing flow completion by 10%, improving throughput by 30%, using 40% less power, incurring 30% less cost, and delivering 50× less downtime than the best-known alternatives.
insights.locator: Google’s implementation

insights.claim: Google credits OCS plus SDN with enabling incremental network builds using heterogeneous technologies and zero-downtime upgrades, meaning the architecture's value is as much operational flexibility as raw efficiency.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous incremental builds let an operator mix generations of accelerators in one fabric — a hidden capex efficiency competitors on rigid fabrics cannot match.
insights.quote: support for incremental network builds with heterogeneous technologies; higher performance and lower latency, cost, and power consumption; real-time application priority and communication patterns; and zero-downtime upgrades
insights.locator: Google’s implementation

insights.claim: Once fiber is installed the network becomes generation-agnostic, since the fiber is indifferent to the transceiver, memory, or processor generation attached to it, so optical plant does not need re-cabling each hardware cycle.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Long-lived optical plant amortizes across multiple GPU generations — improves data-center ROIC math relative to copper re-cabling every refresh.
insights.quote: The fiber has no idea what generation of transceiver or memory or processor is in use, so changing those generations doesn’t require changing the network.
insights.locator: Once an optical network is in place

themes.theme: Hybrid packet/circuit designs and the retrofit case

insights.claim: Operators are evaluating hybrid fabrics in which the top tier of a leaf-and-spine network becomes an OCS while the first layer stays packet-switched, with source routers bundling packets for optical transport and destination routers disassembling them electrically.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: A partial-tier OCS retrofit is a far lower-risk adoption path than a full torus rebuild — the most likely vector for OCS revenue outside Google.
insights.quote: Can we use that technology in leaf and spine structures to replace the second layer with an OCS while keeping the first layer cloud packet switching?
insights.locator: Mixing packet and circuit

insights.claim: Despite the technical enthusiasm, no company outside Google has deployed an OCS network of any topology — the concept remains explicitly exploratory.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Discount any OCS revenue forecast heavily for timing: exploration-phase interest has historically taken years to convert into orders.
insights.quote: It’s more in the exploratory phase right now
insights.locator: This idea is still being mulled

insights.claim: Converting to optical does not require a significant data-center overhaul, so operators can retrofit existing facilities to either cut power draw or add compute capacity within the same power envelope.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Retrofit-without-rebuild is the strongest commercial argument for optics — it monetizes stranded power capacity in existing sites rather than requiring new builds.
insights.quote: If I can retrofit my data centers with this solution, I reduce the power demand, or I can increase capacity in existing data centers.
insights.locator: The initial switchover to optical is manageable

insights.claim: Nvidia has committed $2 billion to Lumentum and another $2 billion to Coherent specifically tied to optical circuit switching, capitalizing the photonics supply chain ahead of any broad OCS deployment.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: A $4B commitment from the dominant accelerator vendor is the strongest available signal that OCS moves from Google-only to merchant architecture.
insights.quote: Nvidia announced a $2 billion investment in Lumentum, and another $2 billion in Coherent for OCS
insights.locator: If this takes off, will it stress optical suppliers

insights.claim: Optical suppliers expect adequate capacity for the next five years based on foundry partners already scaling ahead of anticipated demand plus industry consolidation, arguing against an optics shortage bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Supply-constraint theses on optical components may be overstated — margin expansion from scarcity is less likely than volume-driven growth.
insights.quote: For the next five years, based on our projections, we’re okay
insights.locator: If this takes off, will it stress optical suppliers

insights.claim: Google's OCS implementation is heavily proprietary, and OCP standardization is a precondition for broader adoption — without it, the ecosystem simply will not work.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Track OCP optical working-group output as the gating milestone for merchant OCS revenue; standards ratification precedes volume by design cycles.
insights.quote: Google has developed a lot of proprietary aspects, and it needs to be standardized in order for this to be adopted, or it won’t work right.
insights.locator: Optical standards will help

insights.claim: Lightmatter has joined Nvidia's NVLink ecosystem, an example of photonics startups aligning with the dominant accelerator interconnect rather than competing against it.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Photonics startups that plug into NVLink get distribution; those outside the ecosystem face a much harder path to volume.
insights.quote: Lightmatter recently joined Nvidia’s NVLink ecosystem
insights.locator: Additionally, new alliances are forming

insights.claim: Even proponents concede that production cost and reliability remain unsolved obstacles for optical scale-up, so technical merit alone will not determine adoption timing.
insights.speaker: Bryon Moyer
insights.so_what: Cost and reliability are the two variables to underwrite in optical-interconnect models; a technology that 'makes a lot of sense' can still stall for years on yield.
insights.quote: But with production costs and reliability, there are plenty of challenges to be solved.
insights.locator: Many companies are currently evaluating this option
